---
title: "Train and reuse your first surrogate"
execute:
  eval: false
---

This example uses a bundled SIRDS simulation bank: 100 parameter groups, five
replicates and 40 timepoints. It checks the complete workflow on a CPU.
A short run is not a scientifically validated epidemic surrogate.

## Install

Install [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) and Git.
Python 3.11+ is supported; this example asks uv to manage Python 3.13 for a new
project. You do not need to create or activate an environment yourself.

```bash
uv init my-surrogate --python 3.13
cd my-surrogate
```

On **Linux or Windows**, choose the CPU PyTorch index:

```bash
uv add "torch>=2.10,<3" --index pytorch-cpu=https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
```

The command writes the dependency and named index into `pyproject.toml`.
Set `explicit = true` on that index, and use a platform marker for the torch
source so the same project can use PyPI on Apple Silicon macOS. Replace the generated torch
source and CPU index entries with these entries; do not duplicate the tables:

```toml
[tool.uv.sources]
torch = [
    { index = "pytorch-cpu", marker = "sys_platform == 'linux' or sys_platform == 'win32'" },
]

[[tool.uv.index]]
name = "pytorch-cpu"
url = "https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu"
explicit = true
```

The explicit index supplies torch; unrelated dependencies continue to come from
PyPI. On **Apple Silicon macOS**, use the platform build from PyPI instead:

```bash
uv add "torch>=2.10,<3"
```

Intel Macs are unsupported by the current PyTorch dependency range.

Now add METIS and run the bundled demo:

```bash
uv add "metis-surrogate @ git+https://github.com/OJWatson/metis.git"
uv run metis demo --steps 100 --output metis-demo
```

uv maintains three things for you: `pyproject.toml` records project dependencies,
`uv.lock` records their resolved versions, and `.venv` contains the environment.
Keep the first two with your analysis code. `uv run` uses and synchronizes that
environment, so no manual activation is needed. On another machine, run
`uv sync --locked` in the project and use the same `uv run` commands.

The demo creates `model.pt`, `metrics.json` and `prediction.npy` inside
`metis-demo/`. `model.pt` includes
preprocessing and the ordered input/output schema, so it can be moved to a
machine that does not have the original bank. The package is not yet on PyPI;
the existing `metis` PyPI project is unrelated.

Optional features are recorded with the dependency, so they remain installed
on later `uv run` calls. For figures, pandas tables and tracking:

```bash
uv add "metis-surrogate[plots,pandas,wandb] @ git+https://github.com/OJWatson/metis.git"
```

Choose just the extras you need. To run the Python cells below in a notebook,
add the `[docs]` extra and select the project's `.venv` Python as your notebook
kernel. Include any previously selected extras in the requirement:

```bash
uv add "metis-surrogate[plots,pandas,wandb,docs] @ git+https://github.com/OJWatson/metis.git"
```

Alternatively, save the two Python code cells in one script and run it with
`uv run python my_surrogate.py` from this project directory.

## Train in Python

```{python}
from metis import load_example, Surrogate, TrainingConfig

bank = load_example()
split = bank.split(validation_fraction=0.2, test_fraction=0.2, seed=42)
model = Surrogate("mlp").fit(
    split.train,
    validation=split.validation,
    config=TrainingConfig(steps=500, device="cpu"),
)
report = model.evaluate(split.test)
print(report.by_output)
print(report.worst_groups(5))
model.save("surrogate.pt")
report.save("evaluation.json")
```

A step is an optimizer update, not a full pass through the bank. Validation
chooses the best evaluated model weights. The test set does not influence
scaling, optimization or weight selection. Reserve it for assessing a final
choice; a sweep should use validation for model comparison and assess test
performance only after the choice is made.

## Reload and predict

```{python}
restored = Surrogate.load("surrogate.pt")
prediction = restored.predict({
    "I_0": 0.04, "beta": 0.4, "gamma": 0.15, "omega": 0.02, "mu": 0.02
})
print(prediction.shape)  # (1, 40, 4), original compartment-count units
```

A dict names the inputs; arrays must follow `restored.input_names`. The time grid
and output order are `restored.times` and `restored.output_names`. Extrapolating
outside the training input ranges emits a warning rather than clipping values.

## Use Hydra instead

```bash
uv run metis train model=mlp training.steps=500 training.device=cpu
```

This calls the same `Surrogate.fit` and evaluation methods. Hydra adds
configuration composition, run directories, overrides and sweeps.
See [the Hydra workflow](hydra.qmd).

## Optional CUDA setup

The default example uses CPU. For NVIDIA GPU training on Linux or Windows,
choose a PyTorch CUDA index compatible with your driver and platform using
the [uv guide to PyTorch](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/integration/pytorch/).
For example, **if CUDA 12.8 is appropriate for your machine**, switch the
project's torch source with:

```bash
uv add "torch>=2.10,<3" --index pytorch-cu128=https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
```

Set `explicit = true` on the new `pytorch-cu128` index in `pyproject.toml` and
keep its torch source restricted to Linux and Windows, as in the CPU example.
Use that CUDA index for torch instead of the CPU index. `uv add` updates the
project and lockfile; after any manual source edits, run `uv sync` to update the
resolution. This changes Python dependencies, not the NVIDIA driver.

```bash
uv run python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.cuda.is_available())"
uv run metis train model=mlp training.device=cuda
```

For Python code, set `TrainingConfig(device="cuda")`. CUDA is not available on
macOS, and these setup instructions do not establish that a particular GPU,
driver or precision combination has been validated.
